Q008428:
## Garbage in, garbage out
A model learns the patterns in its data, including errors, duplicates, gaps and inconsistent formats. Data preparation (cleaning, standardizing, deduplicating, labeling where needed) is therefore a prerequisite step that influences all later stages. Model size does not remove the issue.
## Position in the lifecycle
Preparation sits between ingestion and training. Skipping it hurts training results, and problems then show up in deployment as unreliable output.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Bigger models fix it:** larger models can learn flawed patterns just as well, and they do not repair inconsistent records.
- ✗ **B. Only after deployment:** monitoring is important but cannot replace preparing data before training.
- ✓ **C. Data quality drives model quality (correct):** cleaning and standardizing before training is how the pilot's poor results are prevented.
- ✗ **D. Switch to RL:** changing the learning approach does not address defective input data.

## Key idea
Prepare and clean data before training; poor data produces poor models.
Q008429:
## What multimodal adds
Multimodal foundation models process more than one modality: text, images, audio, video and code. For a support tool this means:
- Richer inputs: a screenshot, a photo of a faulty device, a voice message or a log text can be sent together.
- Simpler architecture: one model covers several input types where separate specialized models might otherwise be stitched together.
## Limits to remember
Prompts are still needed, and multimodal models can still make errors (hallucinations), so human review and grounding remain good practice.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. No prompt needed:** instructions are still required to tell the model what to do with the images.
- ✓ **B. Combined inputs (correct):** a screenshot and a typed question together give the model the full context of the problem.
- ✗ **C. Images only:** multimodal models include text, so tickets are used directly.
- ✗ **D. Never wrong:** no gen AI model is error-free, including on images.
- ✓ **E. One model, several modalities (correct):** multimodal models accept different input types, avoiding separate models for each.

## Key idea
Multimodal models take mixed inputs in one model, but they still need prompts and review.
Q008430:
## Two phases
- **Training**: the learning phase. The algorithm processes data and adjusts the model's parameters. It is compute-intensive and happens before the model is used (and again when retraining or tuning).
- **Inference**: the usage phase. The finished model receives new input, such as a prompt, and produces an output. This happens every time a user or application calls the model.
## Why it matters for business
Using an existing foundation model means the provider already paid the training cost; the company pays for inference when it uses the model. Tuning adds a training step for the company.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Reversed:** answering user questions is inference, and learning from the dataset is training.
- ✓ **B. Learn then use (correct):** training is the learning step from data, and inference is applying the learned model to new inputs, which is the sense used in lifecycle and cost discussions.
- ✗ **C. Same step:** they are different phases; only inference involves handling new prompts.
- ✗ **D. Staff training and invoices:** both terms are about the model's operation, not staff education or billing.

## Key idea
Training = the model learns from data; inference = the trained model produces output for new input.
Q008431:
## Modality comes first
The **modality** of a model is the kind of data it takes in and puts out: text, images, audio, video or code. Choosing a foundation model starts with the output the business needs, because a model can only produce what it was built to produce.
- **Large language models** read and write text (and, in many cases, code).
- **Image generation models** (diffusion-based models are the common type) create new pictures from a text description.
- **Multimodal models** accept or produce more than one modality, for example text plus images.
- **Video generation models** create short clips from text or reference images.
## Reading the scenario
Text goes in, but the deliverable is a picture. Matching the output modality is what decides the model type. Google's model catalog on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform (formerly Vertex AI) lets you filter Model Garden by the task you want the model to perform, so you pick a model by what it must produce.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Text-only LLM:** a text model can describe a layout in words but cannot produce the pictures the team wants to review.
- ✗ **B. Speech recognition model:** it converts spoken audio to text, which is a different modality and creates no pictures.
- ✓ **C. Image generation model (correct):** the team supplies a text description and gets new images back, which is the exact input-to-output modality of the use case.
- ✗ **D. Classification model:** it predicts or scores existing items; it does not generate new content, so it creates no images.

## Key idea
Pick the model by the output modality the business needs; text-to-image needs an image generation model.
Q008432:
## Multimodal models
A **multimodal foundation model** can take in and reason across several kinds of data in the same prompt, for example text, images, audio and video. Without one, a team would have to chain separate tools, such as one for reading images and another for writing text, and keep them consistent.
## Reading the scenario
The inputs are mixed (text, photos, a scanned document) and the output is a written summary. The decisive requirement is understanding several input modalities together. Size, audio-only transcription and video generation do not address that.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Video generation:** the adjuster needs a written summary, not a generated replay, and inventing footage from photos would be risky in a claims setting.
- ✗ **B. Small on-device size:** a lightweight model may suit offline use, but the scenario says nothing about offline work, and it does not guarantee the model understands mixed inputs.
- ✗ **C. Audio transcription only:** the inputs are typed text, photos and scans, so a model limited to audio handles none of them.
- ✓ **D. Multimodal capability (correct):** one model can read the description and look at the damage photos and the estimate together, then write the adjuster summary.

## Key idea
Mixed inputs (text plus images plus documents) point to a multimodal foundation model.
Q008433:
## Context window
A model's **context window** is the amount of information, measured in tokens, that it can take into account at one time: your prompt, any documents you include, the conversation so far and the answer it writes. If the input is larger than the window, the model cannot see all of it.
## Why it matters for model choice
- Long documents, long chat histories or many attached files need a model with a window large enough to hold them.
- A larger window helps cross-reference distant sections; it does not remove the need to check the answers.
- Windows differ between models and change as models are updated, so check the current model documentation instead of memorizing a number.
## Reading the scenario
Questions that depend on clauses spread across a long contract require the model to hold the contract in view at once.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Context window (correct):** it sets how much of the contract the model can consider in one request, so a model with a large enough window can relate clauses from different sections.
- ✗ **B. Temperature:** it controls how random or varied the wording is; it does not extend how much text the model can read.
- ✗ **C. Interface languages:** the console language has no effect on how much of a contract the model can process.
- ✗ **D. Image quality:** signature blocks are a minor part of the task; the main need is long-text understanding.

## Key idea
Long documents and long conversations make the context window a key factor in choosing a model.
Q008434:
## Security and data governance as selection criteria
For regulated businesses, **security, privacy and data governance** are often more important than raw model quality. Questions to ask before choosing a model or platform:
- Will the provider train its models on my prompts and data? Google Cloud states that it does not use customer data to train or fine-tune AI/ML models without the customer's prior permission or instruction, and this applies to managed models on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.
- Can I control **where data is processed** and **who holds the encryption keys**? Controls such as data residency choices and customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK) address this.
- Who can access the model and the data (IAM)?
## Reading the scenario
The two stated requirements are no training on provider data and control over processing. Quality rankings and brand familiarity are not compliance controls.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Sharing prompts with other customers:** this is the opposite of the privacy requirement and would expose patient information.
- ✓ **B. Data governance controls (correct):** processing-location and key-management options give the provider the control the compliance team asked for.
- ✗ **C. Leaderboard score:** a high benchmark score shows capability, not that data handling meets healthcare compliance.
- ✗ **D. Brand recognition:** a familiar name is not evidence of any data protection commitment.
- ✓ **E. Training restriction (correct):** a commitment not to train or fine-tune on customer data without permission directly meets the first compliance requirement.

## Key idea
For regulated data, choose on training restrictions and data governance controls, not on benchmark scores or brand.
Q008435:
## Availability, reliability and scale
Once a gen AI feature is customer-facing, it behaves like any production service: it must be up when customers need it, and it must cope with spikes. When comparing models and platforms, ask whether the model is offered as a **managed service**, so that the provider handles serving infrastructure, scaling and operations, or whether your team must host and keep it running.
- A managed API on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform removes the need to maintain model servers.
- Self-hosting an open model gives control but makes your team responsible for capacity and uptime.
## Reading the scenario
"Every hour of every day", "sharp rises in traffic" and "no team to run model servers" describe availability, reliability and scalability.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Audio support:** the scenario does not mention calls; modality does not address uptime or scaling.
- ✗ **B. Longest prompt:** context window affects how much text a request can hold, not whether the service stays available under load.
- ✓ **C. Availability and reliability with a managed service (correct):** Google operates and scales the serving infrastructure, so the bank gets round-the-clock capacity without running servers.
- ✗ **D. Retraining on bank servers:** tuning customizes behavior, but running it on the bank's own hardware adds operational burden and does nothing for traffic spikes.

## Key idea
Round-the-clock, spiky customer traffic calls for a managed, scalable model service.
Q008436:
## Performance, speed and cost trade off
Foundation models come in sizes and tiers. Larger, more capable models handle complex reasoning and open-ended tasks, but they usually respond more slowly and cost more per request. Smaller or "lightweight" tiers are designed for high-volume, latency-sensitive work at lower cost. Google's own model lineup includes both kinds of tier.
## How to choose
- Define what "good enough" means for the task (accuracy, latency, cost per request).
- Start with a smaller tier for simple, high-volume tasks and test it on real samples.
- Move up in capability only if the test shows a gap.
## Reading the scenario
The task is simple (three labels), the volume is high, speed matters and cost must stay low. That favors a smaller, faster model, verified by testing.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. No model:** gen AI models can classify text, and a prompt with the three labels is a common approach.
- ✗ **B. Video generation model:** it is built for creating video, not for labeling text, and parallel capacity is not a reason to use it.
- ✗ **C. Largest model:** it is likely to be slower and more expensive for a simple task, and "always best" ignores the latency and cost limits.
- ✓ **D. Smaller, faster, lower-cost model with testing (correct):** it fits a simple labeling task, keeps latency and per-request cost low at millions of messages, and a sample test confirms the quality.

## Key idea
Match model size to task difficulty; simple, high-volume, latency-sensitive work favors a smaller and cheaper model.
Q008437:
## Customization options in order of effort
Google's guidance on customizing models suggests a staircase:
- **Prompting** a pre-trained model is the quickest, cheapest start. Clear instructions and a few examples often capture tone and format. It suits rapid prototyping and cases with little labeled data.
- **Tuning (fine-tuning)** retrains the model on your own labeled examples so it adapts to your domain, style or syntax. Google recommends starting with prompting and moving to tuning if required to improve results or fix recurring errors. Tuning is most effective when you have a good set of labeled examples whose format matches what the model will see in production.
- **Training from scratch** is a rare choice, needing huge datasets and compute.
## Reading the scenario
The model is accurate but off-brand, and the retailer owns approved examples. That points to prompt design first, tuning second.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Prompt improvement (correct):** it is the fastest and cheapest first step, and brand instructions plus example descriptions often fix tone.
- ✗ **B. Train from scratch:** a few thousand examples are far too little to build a foundation model, and the cost would be huge.
- ✗ **C. Delete the examples:** the approved descriptions are exactly the valuable data that shows the desired voice.
- ✗ **D. Image model:** brand tone in written descriptions is a text task; an image model does not write the copy.
- ✓ **E. Tuning on approved descriptions (correct):** if prompting is inconsistent, adapting the model with the brand editors' labeled examples teaches tone and terminology more reliably.

## Key idea
Customize by prompting first, then tuning on your own good examples; do not build from scratch.
Q008438:
## Four verbs for gen AI use cases
The exam groups business uses of gen AI into what the model does:
- **Create**: generate new content such as text, images, code, audio or video (marketing copy, product images, draft code).
- **Summarize**: condense long material into key points (meeting notes, reports, call transcripts).
- **Discover**: help people find and understand information across large collections, often through natural-language search and question answering.
- **Automate**: take over repeatable tasks or steps in a process, such as drafting routine replies or triaging requests.
## Reading the scenario
Draft code from a plain-language description is new content, so it is code generation under "create". Explaining existing code is an extra assist, but the headline task creates something new.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Summarizing:** condensing code to an abstract is a different task and not what the developers request.
- ✗ **B. Automating payroll:** nothing in the scenario involves payroll, and a draft-code assistant supports developers instead of replacing their workflow.
- ✗ **C. Discovering:** finding existing programs is retrieval; the scenario asks for newly written code.
- ✓ **D. Creating (correct):** the developers get brand-new draft code produced from a description, which is generation of content.

## Key idea
Generating new content from a description, whether text, image, code or video, is the create use case.
Q008439:
## Summarization
**Summarization** uses a model to condense long or numerous items into brief outputs. Calls are first transcribed to text (or processed directly by a multimodal model), then the model writes a short summary per item. The business value is time: people review a paragraph instead of a thirty-minute recording, and managers can spot trends faster.
## Good practice
- Specify the structure you want (issue, action, outcome).
- Spot-check summaries against the source, since models can omit or misstate details.
- Keep people in the loop for decisions based on the summaries.
## Reading the scenario
The need is a short account of each long call. That is summarization.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Automating coaching decisions:** the supervisors still review and decide; a summary supports their judgment and is not a replacement.
- ✗ **B. Creating images:** no images are needed, and calls are not a source for marketing pictures.
- ✓ **C. Summarizing (correct):** each call is condensed into issue, action and outcome, which saves supervisors from listening to full recordings.
- ✗ **D. Discovering location:** the scenario has nothing about locating customers.

## Key idea
Turning long material into short, structured accounts is the summarize use case.
Q008440:
## Discovery
**Discovery** use cases help people find and make sense of information in large collections of content. Instead of keyword matching alone, a gen AI search experience understands the question, retrieves relevant passages from enterprise sources and can write an answer that cites them. Google Cloud offers enterprise search products for this, such as Gemini Enterprise and Agent Search.
## Business value
- Less time spent searching, faster onboarding of new employees.
- Answers that point to source documents, so people can verify them.
## Reading the scenario
Questions in plain language across scattered manuals, with source links, are the textbook discovery case.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Discovering (correct):** employees ask a question and the system finds and explains the relevant content from many sources, with references to check.
- ✗ **B. Closing the department:** nothing here removes the documentation team; the goal is to speed up finding information.
- ✗ **C. Summarizing only:** summaries may be part of an answer, but search-based answers can also include citations to source documents.
- ✗ **D. Creating new manuals:** the manuals already exist; the need is to find answers in them.

## Key idea
Plain-language question answering across large enterprise content, with sources, is the discover use case.
Q008441:
## Automation with a person in the loop
**Automation** use cases let a gen AI system carry out repeatable steps in a business process, such as answering common requests, triaging tickets or filling forms from documents. The model reads the request, uses connected data (such as order status) and acts or drafts a reply.
## Good design
- Automate the high-volume, low-risk requests first.
- Define escalation rules so unusual or sensitive cases go to a person.
- Measure quality and customer satisfaction after launch.
## Reading the scenario
Routine questions answered with order data and exceptions routed to staff describe automation of a service process.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Discovering new customers:** the scenario concerns existing customers' service emails, not prospecting.
- ✓ **B. Automating (correct):** the agent handles the repeatable questions on its own and escalates exceptions, which reduces manual workload.
- ✗ **C. Creating a product line:** the agent writes replies; it does not design products.
- ✗ **D. Summarizing only:** the agent is expected to reply, so one-line summaries would not meet the goal.

## Key idea
Taking over repeatable tasks and escalating exceptions to people is the automate use case.
Q008442:
## Data analysis with gen AI
Gen AI models can translate a plain-language question into a query or calculation, run it against business data and explain the result in words. This **democratizes analysis**: more people can get answers without waiting for an analyst or learning a query language. Typical benefits are faster decisions and less backlog for data teams.
## Cautions
- The answer is only as good as the underlying data (quality, completeness, definitions).
- Results should be checked, especially for decisions with financial impact.
## Reading the scenario
Managers ask a business question and expect an interpreted answer from sales data: natural-language data analysis.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Speech synthesis:** reading out a table is output formatting and gives no analysis or explanation.
- ✗ **B. Image generation:** logos are unrelated to the question about sales performance.
- ✗ **C. Video generation:** producing films does not answer why product lines missed plan.
- ✓ **D. Natural-language data analysis (correct):** the model turns the question into an analysis of the sales figures and explains the finding, so non-specialists can use the data directly.

## Key idea
Asking business questions in plain language and getting interpreted answers from data is the gen AI data analysis use case.
Q008443:
## Structured vs unstructured data
- **Structured data** follows a predefined schema of rows and columns with set data types. It is easy to store in databases or tables and to query with SQL. Examples: customer tables, transaction logs, inventory counts, spreadsheets with fixed columns.
- **Unstructured data** has no predefined data model. Examples: free text such as emails and documents, images, audio, video, scanned pages. It is hard to query with SQL, and historically much of it went unused.
- **Semi-structured data** has some organization (tags or keys) without a rigid table, for example JSON or XML.
## Why it matters for gen AI
Foundation models, especially multimodal ones, can read and generate unstructured content directly, which opens up large archives that traditional analytics could not use.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Revenue spreadsheet:** a fixed set of numeric columns per month is structured.
- ✗ **B. Subscriber table:** columns with set types make this classic structured data.
- ✓ **C. Audio recordings (correct):** sound files have no row-and-column schema, so they are unstructured.
- ✗ **D. Invoice database:** fixed fields for amount, date and customer number follow a schema, so it is structured.
- ✓ **E. Photographs and scans (correct):** images and scanned pages have no predefined fields, so they are unstructured.

## Key idea
Tables with fixed fields are structured; audio, images, video and free text are unstructured.
Q008444:
## Business implications of data type
- **Structured data** is predictable: it can be filtered, joined and aggregated, and its quality problems (missing values, duplicates) are easy to measure.
- **Unstructured data** carries rich context, such as intent, sentiment and detail, but has no schema, so quality is harder to measure. Foundation models are well suited to reading it (summarizing, classifying, extracting facts), which makes archives valuable.
- Both types need **governance**: privacy rules, access control and checks that content is accurate and relevant. Emails and transcripts often contain personal data.
## Reading the scenario
The accurate view recognizes strengths and obligations of each store, rather than ranking one as unusable or exempt from review.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Table unusable, archive ready:** structured data is easily used by AI, and unstructured data is not automatically clean or compliant.
- ✓ **B. Different strengths plus checks (correct):** the table supports precise queries, while the unstructured archive can be understood by foundation models but needs governance and review because it may be noisy or contain personal data.
- ✗ **C. Sentences are structured:** free text has no predefined schema, so it is unstructured.
- ✗ **D. Identical handling:** preparation, access control and quality checks differ with the data type.

## Key idea
Structured data is easy to query; unstructured data is rich but needs governance and quality review before gen AI uses it.
Q008445:
## Labeled vs unlabeled data
- **Labeled data** pairs each example with the answer (the label) the model should learn: an email plus its category, an image plus "damaged" or "intact". It is used in **supervised learning** and in tuning a foundation model to a task.
- **Unlabeled data** has no such answers: raw text, images or logs. It is used to discover patterns (unsupervised learning), and foundation models are pre-trained on very large amounts of it.
## Business implication
Labels usually need human effort and expertise, so labeled data is slower and costlier to obtain, and its quality depends on consistent labeling.
## Reading the scenario
Each email has an agent-written category, which is the answer the model should learn. That is labeled data. Free-text format does not decide labeled vs unlabeled.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Labeled data (correct):** each email is paired with the correct category, giving the model examples with known answers to learn from.
- ✗ **B. Synthetic data:** synthetic means artificially generated; these are real emails with human tags.
- ✗ **C. Streaming data:** describes how data arrives, not whether the answers are attached.
- ✗ **D. Unlabeled:** an email being free text says nothing about labels; here a category tag exists.

## Key idea
Labeled data pairs each example with its correct answer; unlabeled data has no answers.
Q008446:
## Working with little labeled data
Foundation models are pre-trained on very large collections of **unlabeled** data, so they already understand language and many tasks. A business can often skip a big labeling effort:
- **Prompting** with instructions and a handful of examples (few-shot) can be enough for summaries.
- **Tuning** later, if needed, uses a smaller set of high-quality labeled examples. Google's tuning guidance notes that well-labeled data matters more than quantity.
## Reading the scenario
Plenty of raw reports exist, labels do not, and money for labeling is short. Using a pre-trained model with prompts avoids the label requirement.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Wait for full labeling:** a large labeling effort is exactly what the manufacturer cannot fund, and prompting may make it unnecessary.
- ✗ **B. Self-labeling without checks:** unverified labels can repeat errors, and quality of labels is crucial for good results.
- ✓ **C. Pre-trained model plus prompts (correct):** the foundation model already learned from unlabeled data, so a few example summaries in the prompt can produce results without a labeling project.
- ✗ **D. Supervised model from scratch:** supervised learning depends on labeled data, so this contradicts the premise.

## Key idea
Pre-trained foundation models reduce the need for labeled data; start with prompting before investing in labeling.
Q008447:
## Data quality characteristics
Data quality determines how useful and trustworthy gen AI output is. Key characteristics:
- **Completeness**: are required values present? Missing fields reduce what a model can learn or use.
- **Consistency**: is the same thing represented the same way everywhere?
- **Relevance**: does the data relate to the task at hand?
- **Availability / accessibility**: can authorized people and systems reach it when needed?
- **Format**: is it in a form the tools can read?
- **Cost**: what does it cost to collect, store, clean and label?
## Business effect
Poor data quality leads to poor output ("garbage in, garbage out"). Missing values can also skew results if the gaps are not random, for example if one customer group is missing more fields.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Cost:** missing fields do not make data cheaper to use, and cost is not the stated problem.
- ✗ **B. Format:** the storage type is not the problem; the issue is absent values in the records.
- ✗ **C. Availability:** the scenario says nothing about when the data can be read.
- ✓ **D. Completeness (correct):** missing emails, postal codes and birth dates are gaps in required fields, so personalization will be weak or uneven for the affected customers.

## Key idea
Missing values are a completeness problem and weaken or skew what a model can learn from the data.
Q008448:
## Consistency
**Consistency** means the same fact is recorded the same way across records and systems: the same units, spellings, date formats and identifiers. Inconsistent data makes search, joins and model answers unreliable, because "12 oz" and "twelve ounces" look like different items to a program, and a date such as 03/04 can mean two different days.
## Fixing it
- Define standards (units, formats, naming) for the merged data.
- Clean and transform the data to meet the standards, and set rules to keep new data consistent.
- Retest the assistant on known questions.
## Reading the scenario
The same item and date are written in different ways across merged systems. That is a consistency problem.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Consistency plus standardization (correct):** agreeing on one representation for products and dates and cleaning the merged data removes the conflicting answers.
- ✗ **B. Completeness and random values:** nothing is stated to be missing, and inventing values would add errors.
- ✗ **C. Relevance and deleting systems:** the data is relevant to stock questions, and removing it would lose information instead of aligning it.
- ✗ **D. Availability and restarts:** the assistant is running; the answers are wrong because of mixed formats, so restarts change nothing.

## Key idea
Mixed formats for the same fact are a consistency problem; standardize and clean before using the data.
Q008449:
## Relevance and currency
**Relevance** asks whether the data relates to the question the system must answer. For a policy assistant, the useful data is the current, approved HR policy. Marketing brochures and press releases add noise, and old drafts introduce outdated rules that the assistant may repeat with confidence.
## Practices
- Choose sources by task, not by convenience of export.
- Retire or flag outdated content, and name an owner who keeps sources current.
- Test with real employee questions and check against the approved policy.
## Reading the scenario
The data is easy to get but not suitable: off-topic and outdated content.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Format:** the symptoms are off-topic and outdated answers, not unreadable files.
- ✓ **B. Relevance (correct):** the loaded content does not match the leave and benefits task and includes superseded policy, so answers drift or are out of date.
- ✗ **C. Completeness:** a missing title page is trivial; the real issue is that the content is the wrong content.
- ✗ **D. Cost:** exporting has some cost, but cost does not explain irrelevant or outdated answers.

## Key idea
Use data that matches the task and is current; convenient but irrelevant data produces off-topic answers.
Q008450:
## Data accessibility
**Accessibility** (and availability) is about whether the right people and systems can reach the data when they need it. Silos are a common obstacle to gen AI: models and agents that cannot reach the data cannot use it.
## Improving it responsibly
- **Discover and catalog**: know what data exists, who owns it and what it contains.
- **Consolidate or connect** sources in a governed platform (for example a data warehouse or lake on Google Cloud) so they can be found and used consistently.
- **Control access**: grant least-privilege access to approved users, with logging and policies, so data sharing does not become data exposure.
## Reading the scenario
The firm needs faster, wider access without losing control over sensitive customer and contract data.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Catalog and governed platform (correct):** making sources discoverable and available in one managed place ends the weeks-long hunt and keeps oversight.
- ✗ **B. Laptop copies:** scattering copies of customer and contract data creates security and privacy risks and uncontrolled versions.
- ✗ **C. No restrictions:** open access exposes sensitive data and breaks governance rules.
- ✗ **D. Deleting old records:** this shrinks the data without solving access, and may destroy records required for compliance.
- ✓ **E. Access controls and policies (correct):** role-based access lets authorized teams use the data quickly while protecting sensitive content.

## Key idea
Improve accessibility by cataloging and connecting data in a governed platform with proper access controls, not by removing controls.
Q008451:
## Format and cost of preparing data
Data format affects how easily a tool can use it. Clean digital text, tables and common image or document formats are straightforward. Scans, handwriting and mixed file types often need **preparation**, such as text extraction (OCR) or conversion, plus quality checks. Multimodal models and document-processing services can read many of these, but accuracy varies by legibility and layout.
## Business implications
- Preparation takes time and money, and **cost** is part of data quality and accessibility planning.
- Test on a representative sample before committing the full archive, then decide where extra cleaning is worth it.
- Do not discard data by assumption; decide based on its value and measured quality.
## Reading the scenario
The paperwork is valuable but messy. The honest planning answer is to budget for preparation and verify quality early.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Ignore by default:** dropping the oldest or handwritten material without testing may remove the most informative cases.
- ✓ **B. Budget for preparation and test a sample (correct):** mixed formats and scans need conversion and checks, so cost and effort must be planned and quality verified before scaling.
- ✗ **C. No effect:** models do not read every format perfectly, and accuracy on scans and handwriting varies.
- ✗ **D. Cancel:** scanned documents can be processed, so rejecting them outright throws away valuable data.

## Key idea
Messy formats raise preparation cost; plan for conversion and test quality on a sample first.
Q008452:
## Label quality
Labeled data teaches a model what the right answer is. If the labels disagree, the model receives contradictory lessons: the same kind of complaint is both "logistics" and "shipping", so it cannot learn a stable rule. Google's tuning guidance stresses that high-quality, well-labeled data matters more than quantity.
## Practices
- Write clear labeling guidelines with examples and a fixed list of categories.
- Check agreement between labelers on a sample and reconcile differences.
- Make the tuning data reflect what the model will see in production.
## Reading the scenario
Two names for one category is a consistency problem in the labels, and the unpredictable routing fits that cause.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Too few parameters:** nothing in the scenario points to model size, and discarding the data would waste the labeling spend instead of fixing the conflict.
- ✗ **B. Unstructured so tuning cannot work:** free-text complaints are a normal input for tuning language models; the fault is in the labels.
- ✓ **C. Inconsistent labels with shared guidelines (correct):** aligning the category names and reconciling conflicting examples gives the model one clear signal to learn.
- ✗ **D. Too recent:** complaints do not need to age before use, and waiting would leave the same conflicting labels in place.

## Key idea
Inconsistent labels give a model contradictory lessons; fix them with shared guidelines and reconciliation.
Q008453:
## What grounding is
A foundation model answers from patterns learned in training. It has no built-in link to your documents, to today's news or to a licensed data feed, so it can produce fluent text that is wrong (a hallucination). **Grounding** connects the model's output to verifiable sources. Google's documentation lists three benefits: fewer hallucinations, answers anchored to your data sources, and auditability because the response can point to the sources it used.
## What it is not
Grounding does not change the model's weights, does not restrict the model to canned text, and is not a network or hosting setting. It supplies the model with trustworthy material at the time of the request.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Retraining from scratch:** changing weights is training or fine-tuning, a heavier approach. Grounding leaves the model unchanged and adds sources at request time.
- ✗ **B. Isolated infrastructure:** network isolation is a privacy and security choice. It does not make answers more factual.
- ✗ **C. Pre-written answers:** that is a scripted bot. A grounded assistant still generates new text; it simply bases it on retrieved sources.
- ✓ **D. Connecting output to verifiable sources (correct):** the model is given access to specific data, so its answer is tied to that data and can show where it came from, which lowers the chance of invented content.

## Key idea
Grounding ties model output to verifiable sources, reducing hallucination and adding traceability.
Q008454:
## Three kinds of grounding data
Grounding can draw on different places, and the owner of the data matters for access, licensing and freshness:
- **Enterprise data**: content your organization owns, such as policies, manuals, contracts, product catalogs and records in your databases and document stores.
- **Third-party data**: content from outside providers that you license or connect to, such as a market-data feed, a partner catalog or an external search service.
- **World data**: broad public knowledge, such as what a search engine returns for current events and general topics.
## Matching a source to a need
Ask who owns the facts and how often they change. Internal rules are yours. A paid research feed belongs to a provider. Public news is general knowledge that changes daily.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Enterprise, third-party, world (correct):** lending policies are the bank's own content, the research reports come from an external licensed provider, and public regulatory news is general knowledge available on the open web.
- ✗ **B. Swapped roles:** calling internal policies world data and public news third-party data reverses who owns the content.
- ✗ **C. Licensed research as world data:** a feed the bank pays a provider for is third-party data, not open world knowledge, and public announcements are not a licensed provider feed.
- ✗ **D. Policies as third-party:** the bank wrote its own policies, so they are enterprise data, and a paid research feed is not general public knowledge.

## Key idea
Enterprise data is yours, third-party data is licensed from others, world data is public knowledge.
Q008455:
## The RAG flow
**Retrieval-augmented generation** adds a lookup step before the model writes:
1. The user asks a question.
2. A retrieval step searches a knowledge source, often a search index or a vector store of document chunks, and returns the most relevant passages.
3. Those passages are added to the prompt as context.
4. The model generates an answer that uses the supplied material, and the system can show which sources were used.
## Why the output changes
Without retrieval the model relies on training memory alone. With retrieval it works from current, specific text. The weights never change, so new documents are usable as soon as they are indexed.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Voting across models:** comparing several models is an evaluation or ensemble idea. It does not bring in company data and can make several models wrong together.
- ✓ **B. Retrieve then augment (correct):** relevant passages are fetched and placed in the prompt, so the generated answer is based on that material rather than only on what the model memorized.
- ✗ **C. Post-hoc sentence filter:** deleting unmatched sentences after generation does not guide the answer. RAG supplies the sources before generation.
- ✗ **D. Overnight retraining:** RAG does not update the model per question. Fresh knowledge arrives through retrieval, with no training run.

## Key idea
RAG retrieves relevant passages and adds them to the prompt so the model answers from them.
Q008456:
## Grounding adds traceability
Besides accuracy, grounding gives **auditability**: when an answer is built from retrieved sources, the system can return links or references to them. A reviewer can open the manual passage and check the statement. Without retrieval the model's claim comes only from training memory, and there is nothing to point to.
## Settings are not sources
Output length, temperature and safety filters control how long, how varied and how safe a response is. None of them gives the model a verifiable source.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Stricter safety settings:** safety filters block harmful content categories such as hate or harassment, not statements about faults or warranties, and they do not cite anything.
- ✗ **B. Longer outputs:** a longer explanation is still produced from memory and can contain invented reasoning, so it adds words and not evidence.
- ✗ **C. Higher temperature:** more randomness gives more variety and, if anything, more room for error, so it works against verifiability.
- ✓ **D. Grounding with RAG on the manuals (correct):** answers are generated from retrieved passages, and the references let auditors confirm each statement against the original document.

## Key idea
Grounding is what lets an answer point back to its source, so use it when traceability matters.
Q008457:
## Choose the grounding source by where the facts live
Google Cloud offers several ways to ground a model, and the right one follows the data:
- **Grounding with Google Search** connects the model to world knowledge and a very wide range of topics using results from Google's search engine. It suits public, fast-changing information the company does not own.
- **Grounding with Agent Search** and **RAG Engine** connect the model to your own websites and documents.
- Other options connect to existing external indexes, such as Elasticsearch, or to any search API.
## Applying it
Flight disruptions and visa announcements are public and change daily. A snapshot of company files will be stale, and training cannot keep pace. A live search source can.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Fine-tuning on last year's chats:** fine-tuning bakes in past patterns, which are exactly out of date for daily changes, and it gives no sources.
- ✗ **B. Spreadsheet corpus:** a manual copy of visa rules is only as fresh as the last legal review, and it does not cover flight disruptions at all.
- ✓ **C. Grounding with Google Search (correct):** the information is public world data that changes daily, and search results supply current facts together with source references.
- ✗ **D. Brochure data store:** the company's own brochures cannot contain this week's disruptions, and a catalog-driven refresh schedule would be stale on the day it matters.

## Key idea
Public, fast-changing facts call for Grounding with Google Search; your own documents call for RAG over your data.
Q008458:
## Grounding on third-party data
Not all useful data lives in your buckets or on the open web. Google Cloud's grounding options include connecting Gemini to external data sources by grounding with **any search API**, and with an existing **Elasticsearch** index. The model's request is answered with passages the external service returns, while the data stays where its owner keeps it.
## When this is the right fit
- Licensing or freshness means you should not copy the data.
- The provider already runs a search service over the content.
- You want the answer to use their results at request time.
Google Search covers general public information, and Agent Search or RAG Engine ground on data you load into Google Cloud.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Grounding through the vendor's search API (correct):** this grounding option lets the model use results from an external search service at request time, so the licensed content stays with the vendor and is not copied.
- ✗ **B. Uploading everything to Agent Search:** this duplicates a licensed dataset the retailer wanted to leave in place, which can conflict with the license and with freshness.
- ✗ **C. Google Search:** public web results would not contain the vendor's licensed reviews, so the answers would not reflect the licensed content.
- ✗ **D. Fine-tuning then retiring the service:** a sampled fine-tune stores only fragments in weights, goes stale as reviews change and gives no sources.

## Key idea
When a provider already offers a search service over licensed data, ground the model through that external search rather than copying the data.
Q008459:
## Pre-built RAG versus building blocks
Google Cloud gives two routes to RAG over your data:
- **Pre-built RAG with Agent Search**: a managed search-and-answer experience. You point it at websites or documents and it handles ingestion, indexing, retrieval and answer generation, so it is the quicker route.
- **RAG APIs** (RAG Engine): a configurable managed service for developers who want to shape the pipeline, such as how data is parsed and retrieved, and combine it with their own application logic.
## The decision
The trade is speed and low effort against control. Teams that want a working experience quickly choose the pre-built option. Teams building a bespoke application choose the APIs.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Reversed pairing:** the configurable service demands more build effort, which does not meet the first team's speed goal, while the pre-built experience gives the second team little control.
- ✗ **B. Fine-tuning for both:** models can answer from private documents through retrieval without being retrained, and retraining would not give the control over retrieval that team two asks for.
- ✗ **C. Google Search for both:** that grounding source covers public web knowledge, not the agency's private intranet content or document pipelines.
- ✓ **D. Pre-built RAG for team one, RAG APIs for team two (correct):** a fast, managed experience over websites and documents suits the first, and configurable retrieval control suits the second.

## Key idea
Quick managed answers over content point to pre-built RAG with Agent Search; custom pipeline control points to RAG APIs.
Q008460:
## What grounding delivers, and what it does not
The Google Cloud documentation names the benefits of grounding: it reduces hallucinations, anchors responses to your data sources and provides auditability through links to sources.
## Limits to keep in mind
- Grounding does not retrain the model, so documents are used at request time and are not stored in weights.
- The answer is only as good as the sources. Outdated or wrong documents produce outdated or wrong grounded answers.
- Human review stays a good practice for high-stakes content.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Weights hold every document:** grounding supplies data at request time and leaves the weights unchanged, which is what separates it from fine-tuning.
- ✓ **B. Fewer invented answers (correct):** giving the model specific data to answer from reduces the chance that it makes up content.
- ✗ **C. No human review:** grounding reduces risk but does not remove it, and regulated topics still call for human oversight.
- ✗ **D. Perfect knowledge base:** grounding trusts its sources, so gaps and errors in the data show up in the answers. Data quality remains the owner's job.
- ✓ **E. Source links (correct):** grounded responses can point to the passages used, which supports auditability and quick fact-checking.

## Key idea
Grounding reduces hallucination and adds traceability, but it depends on good sources and does not replace review.
Q008461:
## Grounded answers inherit data quality
With RAG the model writes from the passages that retrieval returns. If an obsolete document is in the index, it can be retrieved, and the model has no way to know it has been replaced. The fix is in the data, not in the model:
- Retire or version old documents so that only current ones are searchable.
- Give document owners a process for updating the sources when something changes.
## Why generation settings do not help
Temperature, top-p and safety settings shape how the model writes, not which facts it is given.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Higher temperature:** it adds randomness in word choice, does not change the retrieved passages and makes accurate output less reliable.
- ✗ **B. Strictest safety settings:** safety filters block harmful content categories and do not decide whether a policy document is current.
- ✓ **C. Retire the outdated document (correct):** the stale policy came from the index, so removing it stops retrieval from supplying the replaced rule.
- ✗ **D. Fine-tune on the old policy:** training on the retired text would push the model toward the rule, and fine-tuning is a poor way to fix a stale source.
- ✓ **E. Ownership and review process (correct):** keeping sources current prevents the same problem for the next change, because grounded answers can only be as current as their data.

## Key idea
When a grounded answer is stale, fix the source data and its upkeep, not the generation settings.
Q008462:
## Temperature controls randomness
When a model writes, it picks each next token from a probability distribution. **Temperature** controls how random that choice is:
- **Lower temperature**: the most probable tokens are chosen more often. Output is more focused and predictable. Google describes low values as good for prompts that need a less open-ended or creative response. A temperature of zero always selects the highest-probability tokens, so replies are mostly, but not perfectly, repeatable.
- **Higher temperature**: less likely tokens are chosen more often, giving more diverse and creative output.
## Applying it
Fee explanations need consistency, so lower temperature is right. Combine it with grounding so the facts come from the policy text.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Turning off safety settings:** content filters block harmful categories and do not drive variation between repeated answers.
- ✗ **B. Raising temperature:** higher values make unlikely words more probable, increasing variation, the opposite of the goal.
- ✓ **C. Lower temperature (correct):** favoring the most probable tokens makes repeated asks produce similar, focused answers, which is what consistent fee explanations need.
- ✗ **D. Longer maximum output:** this setting sets a ceiling on length and does not make wording consistent; repeating details would add noise.

## Key idea
Lower temperature for consistent, factual output; higher temperature for diverse, creative output.
Q008463:
## Tuning for creativity
Brainstorming is an open-ended task, so you want variety. Higher **temperature** increases the chance that lower-probability tokens are picked, which leads to more diverse and creative results. Google's guidance also says to try increasing temperature when a model's response is too generic.
## Related controls
- **Top-p** also widens or narrows the pool of candidate tokens.
- **Maximum output tokens** only caps length.
- **Safety settings** only filter harmful content.
Treat creative settings as something to test, and keep human review for brand and legal checks.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Raising temperature (correct):** it lets less likely tokens be selected more often, producing a wider spread of ideas instead of the same predictable ones.
- ✗ **B. Shorter output limit:** it truncates the response and does not change which ideas the model generates.
- ✗ **C. Minimum temperature:** always choosing the most probable token makes output nearly deterministic, which would produce even more repetition.
- ✗ **D. Tighter safety settings:** these filter harmful content and do not push the model toward new phrasing.

## Key idea
Raise temperature for variety and creativity; lower it for focus and consistency.
Q008464:
## Top-p, a second randomness control
After the model scores each possible next token, **top-p** (nucleus sampling) narrows the candidates. Tokens are considered from most to least probable until their probabilities add up to the top-p value, and the rest are excluded. The model then picks among the remaining tokens using temperature.
- A **lower** top-p keeps only the likeliest words, so output is less random.
- A **higher** top-p lets more words compete, so output is more random.
Google's documentation notes that top-p and temperature work together, with temperature applied to the tokens that remain.
## What top-p is not
It is not a length limit, a safety control or a retrieval setting.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Blocking strictness:** harm-category thresholds are the safety settings and are unrelated to token probabilities.
- ✗ **B. Number of passages:** how many passages retrieval returns is a RAG retrieval setting, not a sampling parameter.
- ✗ **C. Token limit:** the maximum number of tokens is the output length setting, which caps how much is written and not how words are chosen.
- ✓ **D. Cumulative probability cutoff (correct):** top-p keeps the smallest set of the most likely tokens whose probabilities sum to the value, and the model chooses among them, so lower values give less random output.

## Key idea
Top-p restricts word choice to the most probable candidates whose probabilities add up to its value.
Q008465:
## Tokens and output length
Models read and write **tokens**, small pieces of text. Google notes that a token is roughly four characters and that 100 tokens are about 60 to 80 words. The **maximum output tokens** setting caps how many tokens a response may contain. When the cap is reached, the model stops, even in the middle of a sentence.
## Fixing truncated answers
- Allow a larger output limit, if the task really needs a long answer.
- Or change the prompt to request a shorter, tighter result, such as a summary within a set number of bullets.
Token count also matters for cost and speed, because longer inputs and outputs use more tokens, so set limits that fit the task and not larger than needed.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Loose safety settings:** safety filters block harmful categories, and loosening or tightening them does not explain a response that stops mid-sentence for ordinary contracts.
- ✓ **B. Output limit too small (correct):** stopping mid-sentence is the sign of a token cap being hit, so raise the limit or ask for a shorter summary so that the full answer fits.
- ✗ **C. Incomplete grounding source:** missing documents would change what the summary says, but the content here is correct and the problem is a cut-off.
- ✗ **D. Low temperature:** temperature changes how random word choice is and does not cut a response off at a fixed point.

## Key idea
A response that ends abruptly usually hit the maximum output tokens limit, so adjust the limit or shorten the request.
Q008466:
## Safety settings
Google's models are designed with safety in mind, but they can still produce harmful responses, especially when prompted to. **Safety and content filters** act as a barrier: you set how aggressively content is blocked for harmful categories (for example hate speech, harassment, sexually explicit and dangerous content). Some protections, such as blocking prohibited content, are always on and cannot be configured.
## Filters versus other controls
- Filters block output, but they do not steer the model's behavior; instructions to the model do that.
- Temperature, output length and grounding shape accuracy, variety and size, not safety.
- For a children's audience, combine stricter thresholds with testing and human oversight, as part of responsible AI practice.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Minimum temperature:** it makes output more predictable but does not stop a model from producing a harmful reply to a harmful request.
- ✗ **B. Shorter outputs:** length does not decide whether the content is harmful, since a short reply can still be unsafe.
- ✓ **C. Safety settings with blocking thresholds (correct):** they are the control that filters potentially harmful categories, so they fit a requirement to block unsafe content for young users.
- ✗ **D. Curriculum-only grounding:** grounding improves factual accuracy but is not a safety filter, and children's typed input can still lead to unsafe replies.

## Key idea
Safety settings are the dial for blocking harmful content; other parameters shape style and length, not safety.
Q008467:
## Match the settings to the task
Two tasks can sit on opposite ends of the same dials:
- **Accuracy-critical tasks** (dosing, legal, finance): ground the model in approved sources, use a lower temperature for focused, repeatable wording, and keep human review.
- **Creative tasks** (newsletters, slogans, ideas): a higher temperature, and possibly a higher top-p, increases variety, with editing before publication.
## Why the length cap is not an accuracy tool
Output length limits how much is written. Cutting it short can remove important qualifiers such as warnings, which is risky for dosing.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Tiny output cap:** truncating to one sentence can drop warnings and conditions and does not make answers more accurate.
- ✓ **B. Higher temperature with editing (correct):** lively newsletters benefit from varied, creative phrasing, and an editor catches problems before release.
- ✗ **C. Ungrounded and high temperature:** this maximizes invention where accuracy matters most.
- ✗ **D. Minimum temperature and top-p:** this makes output near-identical and bland, the opposite of lively newsletter copy.
- ✓ **E. Grounded, low temperature, reviewed (correct):** dosing answers should come from approved documents with focused wording, and a human check suits a high-stakes domain.

## Key idea
Accuracy tasks get grounding and low randomness; creative tasks get higher randomness; length caps and safety filters do neither job.
Q008468:
## Why an agent is more than a model
A language model reads text and produces text. It does not know today's order status, and it cannot place a refund by itself. An **agent** wraps the model in a loop: it reasons about the goal, decides on a step, uses a **tool** to do it, reads the result and continues.
Tools are the agent's bridge to the outside world. The function-calling documentation describes two main jobs:
- **Fetching data**: retrieve up-to-date information, such as an order record or a knowledge-base article, so the answer is current rather than guessed.
- **Taking action**: perform external operations such as submitting a form, updating a record or handing the conversation to a person.
The common tool types in Google Cloud's agent products are API tools (the agent calls an API itself, for example an OpenAPI tool in Conversational Agents), function tools (the model names the call and the client application runs it) and data stores (the agent retrieves from company content).

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Fixed script:** tools do not replace reasoning. The model still interprets the request and chooses which tool to use and with what inputs.
- ✗ **B. Security only:** guardrails and safety settings are separate controls. Tools exist to extend what the agent can know and do.
- ✗ **C. Nightly retraining:** calling a tool does not change the model's weights. Order history is read at the moment of the question, not memorised.
- ✓ **D. Fetching and acting (correct):** tools connect the model to live data and to business systems, so the agent can look up an order and then do something about it instead of only talking.

## Key idea
Tools turn a text-only model into an agent: they fetch current data and take actions in external systems.
Q008469:
## Who runs the call
All tools let a model reach beyond its training. They differ in who executes the call.
- **Function calling** (function tools): the model is given a description of the available functions. When a function is needed, it outputs structured data with the function name and parameters. The documentation is explicit that *your application* then executes the tool and feeds the result back to the model.
- **API tools** (an OpenAPI tool in Conversational Agents is one example): the agent holds the API schema and, by default, calls the API on your behalf. Client-side execution is possible only when it is deliberately configured.
- **Data stores**: the agent retrieves content from indexed company data; they read knowledge, not run business operations.
## Choosing
When the organization wants its own code to stay in control of the call, for example for authorisation, auditing or network location, function calling keeps execution on the client side.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Function calling (correct):** the model only proposes the call, the bank's code makes it, and the model gets the result to finish its answer, which satisfies the rule that the agent platform never touches the banking system.
- ✗ **B. Prompt tuning:** tuning adjusts how the model behaves; it cannot hold current balances, which change constantly.
- ✗ **C. OpenAPI tool:** by default an API tool lets the agent call the API itself, which is exactly what the security team has ruled out.
- ✗ **D. Data store of exported balances:** a data store is searched for content; stale exports are the wrong source for a live balance and it is not a call to the core system.

## Key idea
Function calling = model proposes, your application executes; API tools = by default the agent calls the API itself.
Q008470:
## Data stores as the agent's knowledge
A **data store** tool points an agent at a body of company content. The content is ingested and indexed, so at question time the agent retrieves the most relevant passages and uses them as context. Agent Search data stores can be created from sources such as Cloud Storage and BigQuery, and from website content.
This is the retrieval (RAG) pattern applied to an agent. Updating the knowledge means refreshing the data store, not retraining the model.
## Matching tool type to need
- Questions about documents → data store (read knowledge).
- Looking up or changing a record in a live system → API tool or function tool (take action).
- Calculations or data analysis → a code-execution tool.
The scenario states that only questions over documents are needed and no transactions, so retrieval is the right fit.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Code execution:** running programs helps with calculation and analysis, but the problem here is finding answers inside documents.
- ✗ **B. Browser-run function:** function tools are for calling functionality, not for stuffing documents into prompts, and 4,000 PDFs cannot be pasted into each prompt anyway.
- ✗ **C. Claims API tool:** it takes actions in a live system, which the scenario does not require; it would also not let the agent search policy wording.
- ✓ **D. Data store tool (correct):** it indexes the quarterly documents, retrieves the passages that match each question and keeps answers grounded in the insurer's own content.

## Key idea
Knowledge in documents → data store tool (retrieval); actions in live systems → API or function tools.
Q008471:
## Reading versus doing
Agent tools fall into two broad groups:
- **Knowledge tools** such as data stores: the agent retrieves text from indexed content and answers from it. Nothing outside changes.
- **Action tools** such as API or function tools: the agent, or the application, calls another system to read live state or to change it.
In the plan, three capabilities are questions about published text: packaging rules, contract terms and service-level descriptions. A data store grounded in those documents handles them. Booking a pickup and cancelling a shipment *change records* in live systems, so they need action tools.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✓ **A. Booking a slot (correct):** it writes to the scheduling system, so the agent needs an API or function tool that can make the booking.
- ✗ **B. Service-level differences:** the help-centre text answers the question; retrieval alone is enough.
- ✗ **C. Contract summary:** the agent can retrieve the contract text from a data store and the model can summarise it; no external change is needed.
- ✗ **D. Packaging rules:** they are published text in the handbook, so a data store with retrieval is enough.
- ✓ **E. Cancelling a shipment (correct):** it changes the order management system, which only an action tool can do.

## Key idea
Reading company content → data store; changing or querying live systems → action tools (API, function).
Q008472:
## Speech APIs in an agent's toolbox
Voice agents and call analytics need to move between audio and text. Google Cloud provides two pre-built APIs, one for each direction:
- **Speech-to-Text**: audio in, text out. It supports synchronous requests for short audio, asynchronous (long-running) requests for long recordings and streaming recognition for live audio.
- **Text-to-Speech**: text in, audio out.
Because the APIs are pre-trained and managed, a team calls them as tools without building or training any speech model.
## Applying it
The recordings are existing audio files, and the goal is text. That is transcription.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Vision API:** it analyses images, not sound, and does not identify accents.
- ✓ **B. Speech-to-Text (correct):** it transcribes audio, including long recordings, into text, which is the first step before a model summarises the conversation.
- ✗ **C. Text-to-Speech:** it works in the opposite direction, turning text into spoken audio.
- ✗ **D. Natural Language API:** it analyses text (sentiment, entities, syntax, categories); it does not accept audio and does not transcribe.

## Key idea
Audio → text is Speech-to-Text; text → audio is Text-to-Speech.
Q008473:
## Giving an agent a voice
Text-to-Speech creates synthetic human speech as playable audio from text or from **SSML** (Speech Synthesis Markup Language, which controls pauses, emphasis and pronunciation). The caller chooses a voice, which differs by language, gender and, for some languages, accent. The output is an audio format such as MP3 or LINEAR16.
## Where it fits
It is the output side of a voice assistant: the model writes the answer as text, then the agent calls Text-to-Speech to say it. Accessibility use cases such as reading content aloud are a natural fit.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Translation:** it converts text from one language to another and returns text; it does not generate audio.
- ✗ **B. Speech-to-Text:** it handles the input side, converting the traveller's speech into text; it does not produce speech.
- ✓ **C. Text-to-Speech (correct):** it turns the answer text into spoken audio in a voice and language chosen for the traveller.
- ✗ **D. Document AI:** it extracts structured data from documents; reading aloud is not its function.

## Key idea
An agent speaks with Text-to-Speech and listens with Speech-to-Text.
Q008474:
## The translation options
Cloud Translation has two API editions:
- **Basic**: quick, plug-and-play access to the standard neural machine translation model for text.
- **Advanced**: adds customization and features such as **glossary** support, and document, batch and real-time translation.
**Document Translation** (an Advanced feature) translates formatted files such as PDF and DOCX directly and preserves the original formatting and layout, instead of returning plain text. A glossary lets the firm define how particular terms must always be translated.
## Why this matters for agents
An agent that translates documents can use the API as a tool and hand the file back, rather than asking a model to retype and reformat it.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Speech-to-Text:** it converts speech to text; reading documents aloud is a needless round trip and does not translate.
- ✗ **B. Natural Language API:** it analyses text, for example finding entities, but it is not a translation service and does not rewrite documents.
- ✓ **C. Translation - Advanced (correct):** Document Translation keeps tables and headings in the translated DOCX and PDF files, and the glossary enforces the firm's approved legal terms.
- ✗ **D. Translation - Basic with pasting:** Basic does not offer glossaries or document translation, and pasting paragraphs loses the layout the firm needs.

## Key idea
Formatted-document translation with enforced terms → Cloud Translation Advanced (Document Translation and glossary).
Q008475:
## Unstructured documents to structured data
Document AI is a document processing and understanding platform. It takes unstructured data from documents and transforms it into **structured data**, such as specific fields suitable for a database. It works through **processors**:
- **Digitize**: OCR to get text and layout.
- **Extract**: form parsers, custom extractors and pretrained parsers (for example, for invoices and receipts).
- **Classify**: custom classifiers and splitters that identify document types.
It can also store results in products such as Cloud Storage and BigQuery.
## Agent angle
Document AI is the tool an agent calls when the input is a document and the output must be fields, not prose.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Natural Language sentiment:** it scores the emotional tone of text, which is irrelevant to invoice fields.
- ✓ **B. Document AI (correct):** its processors read scanned and PDF invoices, identify the fields and line items and return them as structured data the finance system can ingest.
- ✗ **C. Text-to-Speech:** audio is not the goal, and a spoken invoice gives the finance system nothing to ingest.
- ✗ **D. Translation Basic:** it returns translated text, not structured fields, and does not parse layout or line items.

## Key idea
Documents in, structured fields out → Document AI.
Q008476:
## What the Vision API offers
Cloud Vision API is a pre-trained service for understanding images. Its features include:
- **Label detection**: generalised labels for the image, each with a confidence score.
- **Object localization**: objects with bounding boxes.
- **Logo and landmark detection**.
- **Text detection** (OCR) and dense-document text detection.
- **Explicit content detection** (SafeSearch).
- Face detection and web entities.
Using it means no model training: the marketplace sends the image and gets structured results back.
## Vision versus Document AI
Vision's OCR reads text in an image. Document AI goes further for business documents: it extracts named fields and entities. For product photos the Vision API is the right tool.

## Why each option works or fails
- ✗ **A. Speech-to-Text:** photos have no audio track, and it processes speech, not images.
- ✗ **B. Natural Language API:** it analyses text; it cannot examine pixels.
- ✗ **C. Document AI:** it is aimed at documents and their fields and entities, not photographs of products and brand logos.
- ✓ **D. Vision API (correct):** label, logo and SafeSearch features cover all three needs with a ready-made API.

## Key idea
Photo labels, logos, text and explicit content → Vision API; business-document fields → Document AI.
Q008477:
## Text analysis without training a model
The Natural Language API analyses text. Its methods include:
- **Sentiment analysis**: whether the writer's overall attitude is positive, negative or neutral.
- **Entity analysis**: finds proper and common nouns, such as places, people and amenities.
- **Entity sentiment analysis**: combines the two, giving the opinion about each named entity.
- **Syntactic analysis** (sentences and tokens) and **content classification** (categories).

## Managing agents centrally
Gemini Enterprise gives administrators one place to oversee agents from Google, third parties and internal teams. Each agent has a state:
- **Enabled**: active and usable by authorized users.
- **Private**: for personal use; only its creator can chat with it.
- **Suspended**: temporarily deactivated. It remains visible in the Agent Gallery with a message explaining the deactivation; users cannot interact with it, but owners and admins keep full access.
- **Disabled**: inactive and hidden from the Agent Gallery until the owner or an admin re-enables it.

- ✓ **A. Suspended (correct):** the agent is deactivated for users, yet still listed with a message, and the owner and admins can keep working on it.
- ✗ **B. Deleted:** removal takes the agent off the Agents page and the web app, so it cannot be fixed and users get no explanation.

- ✗ **D. Enabled:** the agent would stay in use, which is what the administrator wants to stop.
